profile.summary: 2 Timothy is Paul's farewell, written of the Roman prison when he realizes that his missionary career was coming to an end. Instead of just defending or lamenting, he entrusts Timothy to continue the work of the gospel with courage, fidelity, and perseverance. The letter has a personal and urgent tone: Paul knows that his end is near, but he insists that the mission of God will continue through faithful servants. The book combines apostolic example, resistance to suffering, care for sound instruction and hope in the final consummation.
profile.setting: The letter is located at the end of Paul's life during a second prison in Rome, more severe and probably linked to his execution. Timothy seems to be in the province of Asia, possibly in Ephesus, and Paul calls him to travel to Rome as soon as possible. The background includes the previous expansion of Paul's ministry throughout the Roman world, his first imprisonment, subsequent release and new imprisonment. Pauline authorship is assumed by the introduction, but the exact date remains debated; the evidence pointed out favors the second arrest in Rome, near Paul's death.

structure.label: Greeting and the initial call
structure.description: Greeting, thanksgiving and Paul's first exhortation for Timothy to suffer for the gospel with fidelity and courage.

structure.label: Strengthening for the Ministry
structure.description: Paul renews the charge: Timothy must persevere, avoid useless contention and lead his service amid opposition and false teachers.

structure.label: The Difficult Times and Scripture
structure.description: The prospect extends to the last days, marked by difficulties; Timothy must stand firm in the faith received and in the Scriptures.

structure.label: Conclusion, appeal and farewell
structure.description: Paul asks for Timothy's presence in Rome, gives news and greetings, reaffirms that his mission is completed and ends with blessing.

themes: hope amidst the opposition and the end of life
readingKeys: Notice how Paul transforms his own prison into a model of fidelity and hope for Timothy.
Note the passage from the personal burden to the broader view of spiritual conflict and the last days.
Follow the repeated references to Paul's example, which function as a concrete stimulus for perseverance.
profile.cautions: The introduction is more likely that the letter was written during Paul's second prison in Rome, but acknowledges that some hold a previous date. There is also uncertainty as to the exact details of the second incarceration and the role of certain opponents. The reader should note that these historical questions are treated as probable, not absolutely right.

dossier.narratedEra: The narrated time is the end of Paul's life during his second prison in Rome, with a probable expectation of imminent execution. The letter imagines Paul already in the outcome of the ministry, calling Timothy the province of Asia, probably Ephesus, to go to Rome as soon as possible. The narrative background includes suffering, judgment, abandonment by some, opposition of false masters and the proximity of winter, which affected sea trips.
dossier.compositionEra: The composition is traditionally attributed to Paul, written from Rome in his second prison, when he was in danger of life. The notes also recognize that there was discussion about a possible date in the first Roman prison, but consider the evidence stronger for a later date, linked to Paul's death. Matthew Henry states that this was the last epistle written by Paul. The sources provided do not present an absolute date, only that relative sequence.

politics.title: Roman prison under imperial authority
politics.detail: The letter is located in Rome, with Paul imprisoned and taken to the imperial court; Matthew Henry mentions that he was brought before Emperor Nero, and Tyndale describes a second prison in Rome culminating in Paul's death.
politics.readingImpact: This gives the book the tone of apostolic will and causes the exhortation to perseverance to be read in the shadow of imperial power and the real threat of execution.

politics.title: Roman Judgment in two stages
politics.detail: Tyndale notes that Paul probably refers to the first phase of a Roman judicial hearing, distinct from the trial itself.
politics.readingImpact: This helps to read the procedural references of 4:16 without imagining a single simple process; the text is born from a concrete and tense legal situation.

politics.title: Roman Empire as a scene of opposition
politics.detail: The sources indicate that Paul was imprisoned in Rome and that his defense before the authorities became an opportunity for proclamation of the gospel; Tyndale also associates Timothy's suffering with the persecution that he could accompany him when traveling to Rome.
politics.readingImpact: Reading begins to consider the gospel in confrontation with imperial structures, not just as an inner or devotional message.

politics.title: Possible involvement of opponents in the crisis
politics.detail: Tyndale says that the details of Paul's second prison are not known, but suggests that Alexander may have participated in the arrest, and that the false masters were still active.
politics.readingImpact: This connects Paul's prison and martyrdom to the doctrinal conflict in and around the churches, making the letter also a document of ecclesial dispute.

customs.title: Fight, tears and farewell among co-workers
customs.detail: Tyndale interprets Timothy's tears as a sign of a previous farewell, possibly when Paul was transferred to Rome under prison.
customs.readingImpact: Personal affection is not an embellishment: he shows that Paul's exhortation is born of real bonds of discipleship and mission.

customs.title: Ordination with laying on of hands
customs.detail: Tyndale's note about 1:6 associates the laying on of hands by Paul and the elders to Timothy's ordination to the ministry.
customs.readingImpact: The reader understands 2 Timothy as a letter of ministerial continuity, not just personal comfort; there is a public and recognized charge.

customs.title: Travel before winter and maritime logistics
customs.detail: Paul asks for Timothy's arrival before the winter; the note explains that the navigation for the Adriatic closed from November to March and that the lack of a coat would be a problem in prison without heating.
customs.readingImpact: The letter wins daily concreteness: the request by company, clothing and travel time shows physical vulnerability and pastoral urgency.

customs.title: Rich house and utensils as social image
customs.detail: Commenting 2:20-21, Tyndale uses the image of utensils in a rich house to show honor and dishonor within God's house.
customs.readingImpact: This guides community reading: purity and ministerial utility are compared to domestic objects of unequal value, in a recognizable everyday life frame.

customs.title: Practice of meals and sacrificial offer as a metaphor
customs.detail: Paul describes his death as a degrandmed libation, and Tyndale connects this image to offers of the veterotestamentary cult.
customs.readingImpact: The death of the apostle is read as an act of worship, not only as a biographical end; the reader sees his own life as offered to God.

language.title: Included from the Spirit in 1:6-7 and 1:14
language.detail: Tyndale states that allusions to the Spirit in these verses form an inclusion, or literary frame, around the section.
language.readingImpact: This highlights the rhetorical unity of the exhortation: courage, gift and fidelity are framed by the work of the Spirit.

language.title: The image of the entrusted "deposit"
language.detail: The note explains that "guardare entrust" and "deposit" belong to the same verbal field, describing the apostolic truth as something entrusted and to be preserved.
language.readingImpact: Reading begins to emphasize custody responsibility, not doctrinal creativity; Timothy must guard and also transmit.

language.title: "Enduring suffering" as a theme of education
language.detail: Tyndale says that in 2:1-13 Timothy is again called to be strong and to suffer with Paul, with obedience motivated by the memory of the gospel and the example of Paul.
language.readingImpact: Suffering is not accidental; it is presented as part of the pattern of discipleship and apostolic succession.

language.title: "Guide straight" in the interpretation of truth
language.detail: The expression of 2:15 may mean correctly interpreting the word of truth, or remaining in the purpose of teaching without deviating to controversies.
language.readingImpact: The focus of the text is pastoral and hermeneutic: fidelity to the truth includes direction, discipline and refusal of empty discussions.

language.title: "Word of God is not imprisoned."
language.detail: Tyndale reads 2:9 as a contrast between Paul's physical prison and the freedom of the gospel, which remains victorious by the power of Christ's resurrection.
language.readingImpact: The image strengthens the letter as a testimony of resistance: the apostle's body may be trapped, but the message does not.

language.title: Crown/victors crown and epiphany
language.detail: In 4:1-8, 4:8, Tyndale highlights the victor's judgment, appearance and crown vocabulary, linking eschatological expectation to ethical perseverance.
language.readingImpact: Language begins to structure missionary urgency and future hope; the present service is read in the light of Christ's appearance.

timeline.title: Conversion of Paul and missionary expansion
timeline.detail: Tyndale summarizes Paul's arc of ministry from his conversion to Acts 9 to his extensive work in Jerusalem, Asia Minor, Ephesus, and Italy.
timeline.readingImpact: The reader perceives 2 Timothy as the closure of a long apostolic trajectory, not as an isolated episode.

timeline.title: First prison in Jerusalem, Caesarea and Rome
timeline.detail: The introduction traces the prison sequence in Jerusalem, detention at Caesarea and imprisonment in Rome, before a later release and new ministry.
timeline.readingImpact: It helps distinguish the previous 2 Timothy scenario from the first Roman chain and avoids confusing the phases of Pauline life.

timeline.title: Possible period of ministry after first imprisonment
timeline.detail: Tyndale states that Paul was later released and wrote 1 Timothy and Titus in that interval before the new prison in Rome.
timeline.readingImpact: This situates 2 Timothy as the last piece of a pastoral set after the first liberation, reinforcing its final tone.
timeline.reference: 2Tm 1:8, 16-17; 2:9; comparison with 1Tm and Tt according to introduction

timeline.title: Writing in the final episode of Paul's life
timeline.detail: Tyndale says that the letter came during the conclusive episode of Paul's life, and Matthew Henry describes it as writing when his withdrawal from this world was near.
timeline.readingImpact: The reading of the letter gains weight of apostolic farewell and legacy to the church.

timeline.title: Possible date in the first prison, but preference for a second prison
timeline.detail: The date section recognizes the possibility that 2 Timothy was written in the first Roman prison, but says that the evidence strongly supports a later date in the second prison.
timeline.readingImpact: The interpreter should read with caution any rigid chronology; the note itself records alternative and preference, without closing the debate with exact date.

timeline.title: Audience before Nero and "first defense"
timeline.detail: Matthew Henry claims that Paul had been brought before Emperor Nero and that 4:16 describes his first defense when he was abandoned.
timeline.readingImpact: This data reinforces the legal scene and the isolation of the apostle, making the letter a text of resistance under state pressure.

investigation: The notes do not provide independent historical details of Paul's second prison; they only presuppose it and bind it to the apostle's death.
Timothy's exact location at the time of writing is not certain; Tyndale suggests the province of Asia, probably Ephesus, but treats this as inference from 4:13, 19.
There is internal debate in the notes on the date of composition: a possibility is the first Roman prison, but the preferred reading is the second prison.
The hypothesis that Alexander participated in Paul's arrest is only suggestive in the notes, not a proven statement.
Some social details cited in 4:21, such as names of brothers and sisters and the later identification of Linus, are mentioned incidentally and do not structure the main chronology.
dossier.limits: This dossier depends solely on the annexed notes of Tyndale and Matthew Henry, without using external historical reconstructions. Therefore, there are real gaps: the exact civil chronology does not detail, the involvement of characters such as Alexander is not proven independently, and the possible presence of Timothy in Ephesus remains inferential. The notes are also selective: they emphasize suffering, ministerial succession, Roman judgment, opposition of false teachers and pastoral images, but they hardly deal with economics, social classes or urban life in addition to some punctual signs such as travel, prison, rich house and names of cooperatives. Where the source presents interpretive alternatives, they were marked as debated or interpretation, without solving questions that the material itself does not solve.
